source.title: [Paper] A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: This is a high-level LessWrong summary with comments, not the technical paper; it directs readers to the arXiv paper for details.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports results that refine the claim about interpretability: SAE latents that appear to track a feature can miss qualifying examples, and the authors describe them as unreliable classifiers.
record.gate_note: The post says the study tested over 200 Gemma Scope SAEs on first-letter identification and compared their tracking of character information with linear probes. It gives no precision or recall values, per-SAE results, or detailed intervention results. Claims and results cited from other work, and discussion comments about additional examples, are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study measures Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latents in Gemma-2-2b, not the model's own neurons. Every version is about neurons, or neuron explanations in V6/V7. Bloom says the work concerns measurement error in the SAE method, not how models work. The finding, latents that look interpretable but miss qualifying examples, is analogous to V6 but uses a different unit. It belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress this is measurement error in the SAE method, not a property of how the model itself represents spelling. Linear probes recover the letter information well. They attribute absorption to sparsity training where dense and sparse features co-occur, and expect it to affect sparse feature circuits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE latents and first-letter classification with known labels, rather than auditing neuron poles or testing neuron explanations written from activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The post says absorption varies with SAE size and sparsity, but supplies no setting-specific results.

fits_no_version.finding: In over 200 Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs on Gemma-2-2b, latents that appear to track first-letter features are unreliable classifiers, much worse than linear probes. They miss tokens whose letter information is absorbed by token-aligned latents, which causally mediate in their place.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents that appear interpretable can be unreliable classifiers because of feature absorption, so an inspection-based interpretation of an SAE latent overstates its coverage.

record.problems: The post is a high-level summary and omits numerical precision and recall, per-SAE results, uncertainty estimates, and details of the causal interventions. The reported evidence concerns one model, one SAE architecture (JumpReLU), and one task (first-letter identification).
record.rows_left_out: No additional study-result rows were available in the summary. Commenters’ examples and results attributed to other work were excluded.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron poles in Qwen3-32B.
No neuron-share comparison across models or scale.
No test of architecture or tools on neuron interpretability share.
No neuron-based attribution graphs. The study argues absorption hampers sparse SAE-feature circuits, not neuron circuits.
Tests SAE latents with ground-truth labels, not neuron explanations written from activating examples.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The source is a LessWrong summary of arXiv 2409.14507. Quantitative precision and recall values are in the paper, not the post. Because it concerns SAE latents rather than neurons, it bears on no version as stated. The reader's 'supports V6' label is dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests SAE latents, not the share of neuron poles with one or two main jobs or the share not understood.
No comparison across language models, architectures, or model scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No vision-model estimate or test of how architecture, regularization, and tools affect interpretability.
No attribution-graph test using a model's own neurons.
The study assesses SAE-latent tracking of first-letter labels, not explanations written from activating examples for individual neurons.
No explainer-model scoring by simulating neuron explanations on new text, and no reported share of neurons with good scores.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Measured how SAE latents tracked first-letter information using precision and recall on a first-letter identification task.

conditions.value: over 200 Gemma Scope SAEs; aggregate summary

rows.measure: Precision and recall of SAE latents tracking first-letter information
rows.baseline: Linear probes; the post says they performed much better
rows.value: The post describes SAE latents as quite unreliable classifiers, much worse than linear probes; no precision or recall values are given.
rows.locator: TLDR; section beginning “To answer these questions”
rows.note: The post reports an aggregate result for over 200 SAEs but does not provide per-SAE values or the numerical precision and recall.
rows.check: Subject is SAE latents trained on Gemma-2-2b, not neurons. V6 names neuron explanations from activating examples. No precision or recall numbers are given, so the value is only qualitative.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Identified feature-absorption cases in which an SAE latent appears to track a first-letter feature but fails on some qualifying tokens, while another latent takes over that feature information and causally mediates instead.

conditions.value: Gemma Scope; over 200 SAEs tested overall

rows.measure: Whether apparently feature-tracking SAE latents fire on qualifying examples; causal mediation by absorbing latents
rows.value: The post reports that some apparently interpretable latents fail to activate on seemingly arbitrary qualifying examples, while absorbing latents weakly project onto the feature direction and causally mediate in place of the main latent.
rows.locator: TLDR; section “Feature splitting vs feature absorption”
rows.note: The summary gives no counts, per-latent results, or details of the causal intervention.
rows.check: Feature absorption describes SAE latents, not model neurons, so it does not measure what V6 names. No counts or intervention results are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2b SAE latents on the first-letter identification task
reader_labels.reason: The reported unreliable classification and feature-absorption false negatives show that an apparent feature interpretation can fail to cover qualifying examples (r1, r2).
